units: the caretaker unlocks the courtyard gate at sunrise
the courtyard floor is swept in front of the mailboxes
the planters under the awning are watered after the sweeping
parcels are stacked against a wall around midday
the children of the building use the courtyard as a play area in the afternoon
the children's racket is tolerated until dusk
a single lamp with chipped glass lights the way to the stairs
the gate is shut again and the emergency exit checked before night
this arrangement has never been set down in any written rule
text: At sunrise the caretaker unlocks the gate, and the inner courtyard wakes up slowly. He sweeps the rough paving in front of the mailboxes, pushing the grit toward the drain. Then he waters the two planters that sit under the awning. By midday the delivery drivers have stacked parcels against the far wall, and the passage narrows into a cluttered corridor. In the afternoon the children of the building take the yard over, rolling a ball from step to step, and he puts up with the racket until dusk. Once the windows light up one by one, the quiet comes back. A single lamp, its glass chipped, throws a thin beam over the way to the stairs. Before night falls he shuts the gate again and checks the emergency exit. Nobody has ever set this routine down in writing, yet it comes around the same way every day.

units: repairing an appliance now costs more than buying another one
the steep price of spare parts puts people off going to a repairer
appliances in working order are thrown into the sorting bins
the pile-up of discards raises the bill for treating waste
that expense is carried by the community
the cheapest choice for one person brings the heaviest cost for everyone
bringing the price of parts down would be part of the cure
making repair manuals available is the second measure put forward
text: Getting a broken appliance fixed now costs more than buying another one, and that reversal has quietly reshaped what we do. Spare parts sell at a steep price, so the owner gives up on the repairer the moment a lid cracks or a handle works loose. The outcome sits in plain view in the sorting bins, where machines barely worn lie beside wobbly chairs that a screwdriver would have saved. All that discarded metal and plastic pushes up the bill for treating waste, and the community foots it in the end. So the loop closes. The cheapest choice for one person turns into the heaviest expense for everyone. Breaking it would mean bringing the price of parts down and putting repair manuals within reach of anyone who asks for them. Until that happens, a workshop where things get mended will stay an oddity.

genre: portrait / biographie (personne désignée par son rôle)
units: a neighbor mends the other tenants' clothes for nothing
she has sewn since she was a teenager and was never trained
her sewing machine came down from her mother
the table holding the machine wobbles and is propped up with cardboard
the ceiling light was too weak to tell a dark thread from a dark cloth
the poor light made her seams go wrong
a tenant from downstairs found her an adjustable lamp at a secondhand market
the lamp gathers the beam exactly where it is needed
she refuses to be paid and asks for a hot drink instead
text: Every stairwell seems to have one, the neighbor who takes in everybody's torn clothes and hands them back mended, without asking for a thing. She has been sewing since she was a teenager, and nobody ever taught her. The machine came down from her mother, and it stood on a wobbly table she kept level with a folded piece of cardboard. Light was her trouble. The ceiling bulb burned too dull to separate a dark thread from a dark cloth, so her seams wandered off and she had to unpick them and start over. A tenant from downstairs turned up with an adjustable lamp he had found at a secondhand market, its shiny reflector gathering the beam right where her hands were. Now a frayed hem takes her two stitches. She waves the money away, asks for a hot drink, sits down and tells workshop stories, and the whole corridor gains by it.

units: two food shops stand face to face at the entrance to the neighborhood
the first one fills a cramped and badly heated room
the fruit in the first shop is weighed by hand
the owner of the first shop calls out his prices
the second one carries a far wider range and clear labels
the second one offers a checkout with no employee
the fruit from the cramped shop has a straightforward smell
the fruit from the shop next door is even but tastes of nothing
the shopper settles it by mood and hardly ever by reason
text: Two food shops stand face to face at the entrance to the neighborhood, and the contrast is worth a pause. The first one fills a cramped, badly heated room where crates climb toward the ceiling. The fruit gets weighed by hand and the owner calls out his prices across the counter. The second one gleams behind its windows, with a far wider range, labels you can actually read, and a checkout where no employee stands. Use them both for a while and the gap in quality turns out not to follow the gap in comfort. Tomatoes from the cramped room ripen on the shelf and smell of something. The ones next door are firm, even in size, and taste of nothing at all. On one side you pay for discomfort and flavor, on the other for ease and blandness. Shoppers settle it by mood, hardly ever by reason.

units: the writer of the letter writes from the table where the meals were eaten together
the floor by the window is cracked and has not been replaced
the rug in the hall has lost its fringes
the teapot chipped at the spout is still used every evening
one armrest of the chair is worn down to the weave
a shawl left behind by the reader lies on that chair
the drawer holds keys, postcards and a worn stub of pencil
the plants on the ledge hang on despite careless watering
the door creaks and still shuts badly
text: I am writing from the kitchen, at the table where the two of us used to eat. Nothing here has changed, and that is precisely what I wanted to describe. The tiles beside the window remain cracked. I abandoned any idea of replacing them, since they belong to the room now. The hallway rug has lost its fringes, and I step over it without noticing. That teapot you detested, chipped at the spout, still appears every evening. One armrest of the armchair is worn down to the weave, and the shawl you left behind lies across it. The drawer holds your keys, a stack of postcards, and a pencil worn to a stub. On the outside ledge the plants survive my careless watering. I tidy very little, as you know. But I keep these battered objects the way you keep familiar handwriting. Come back whenever you like. The door creaks, and it shuts no better than before.

units: a dark ring low on a partition wall points to damp coming through
what to do about it depends on how far it has gone
at the first stage the plaster darkens but still feels dry to the touch
airing the room and pulling away the furniture that blocks the air is enough at that stage
a cheap measuring device confirms the trend
the coating turns spongy and gives under pressure as the damp works inward
the wall then has to be tapped and a seal or a pipe checked
at the late stage the plaster lifts away in patches
painting over it hides the sign without removing the cause
text: What should you do when a dark ring creeps up the bottom of a partition wall? It depends on how far the damp has already gone. Early on, the plaster darkens without coming loose, and the surface still feels dry under your fingers. Open the windows, pull away the cabinet that blocks the air, and that will usually do it. A cheap moisture meter confirms the trend in a couple of readings. Later, as the damp works inward, the coating turns spongy and gives under light pressure. Now you have to tap along the wall, trace the water back, and check the seal of a joint or the run of a pipe. At the late stage the plaster lifts away in patches and leaves a gritty face behind. Treating the surface will not do any more. And painting over it? That hides the sign and lets the damage work on underneath.

units: a tenant reports to the manager a dripping tap going back to the fall
the manager points to the lack of a written request
the tenant says he called three times and got no answer
the manager grants that the switchboard was swamped and the messages went missing
with no report on record no tradesman was sent out
the drip therefore carried on and stained the ceiling of the home below
the tiles under the sink have split
the repair will run higher than a seal changed at the start
the two settle on confirming every call in writing the same evening
text: The tenant told the manager that the tap in the washroom had been dripping since the fall. The manager answered that no written request had ever reached his desk, and that nothing gets ordered without one. The tenant reminded him he had called three times and never got hold of anyone. The manager granted that the switchboard had been swamped and those messages had gone missing. With no report on record, he said, no tradesman had been sent out, so the drip had simply carried on. The tenant pointed out that the ceiling of the home below now carries a brown ring, and that the tiles under the sink have split. The manager conceded that the repair would run higher than a seal changed back at the start. The two settled on a rule, that every call gets confirmed in writing the same evening.

genre: texte historique de vulgarisation (sans époque nommée)
units: before running water every household had to fetch its water outside
the chore fell mostly to the children and to the servants
the buckets were carried up worn and slippery steps
the water stood in containers nobody scoured properly
illness passed from one person to another through this stored water
the local authorities began by opening more places to draw water
that step shortened the walk without making anything cleaner
piping under pressure together with treatment settled the problem
putting a tap in the kitchen did away with the household store
text: Before water ran into homes, every household sent someone out to a well or to a fountain in the neighborhood to fetch it. The chore fell mostly to the children and to the servants, who hauled heavy buckets up steps worn smooth and often slick. Tiredness was the smaller part of the trouble. The water stood for days in containers nobody scoured properly, slimy at the bottom, and illness passed from one person to the next through it. Local authorities began by opening more places to draw from. That shortened the walk, but it left the stored water no cleaner. What settled the matter was piping under pressure, together with treatment of the supply before it reached the houses. Once a tap stood in the kitchen, the household store vanished, and the main source of contamination went with it.

units: bread and a dry cracker left out overnight change in opposite directions
the bread goes hard while the cracker goes limp
the single cause behind both changes is water on the move
fresh bread holds a great deal of water, most of all in the crumb
the water in the bread drifts off into the room and the starch settles anew
the cracker comes out of the oven with almost no water
the cracker pulls moisture in from the air and loses its snap
a damp cloth laid over the basket keeps the crumb supple
shutting the two foods away brings about two opposite effects
text: Leave a slice of bread and a dry cracker out on the table overnight, then look at what has happened. The bread has gone hard and the cracker has gone limp, two opposite outcomes with one cause behind them, water on the move. Fresh bread holds a great deal of it, most of all in the crumb. That water drifts off into the air of the room, the starch settles into a different arrangement, and the crumb is left dry and brittle. The cracker comes out of the oven with almost none, so it absorbs moisture from the air instead, its sugars soften, and the snap gives way to a spongy limpness. Each one reaches for a balance with whatever surrounds it. A damp cloth laid over the basket keeps the crumb supple. Shut the bread away to hold its water in, shut the cracker away to keep water out. One tin, two opposite jobs.

units: a bunch of keys was left behind on a low wall near a bus stop
a student photographed it and then handed it in at the kiosk nearby
the kiosk keeper listed the objects hanging from the ring
the ring carried a mailbox key and a token for a cart
a building badge with nothing written on it hung there as well
the photograph stayed up on the kiosk window for two evenings
the neighborhood put forward several guesses about who owned it
the caretaker of a block knew the badge model and worked out the floor
the owner had not yet noticed that her keys were missing
text: It started with a bunch of keys left behind on the low wall by a bus stop. A student photographed them, and then took them along to the kiosk a few steps away. The kiosk keeper laid out everything hanging from the ring, a mailbox key, a dull token for a cart, a scuffed leather fob, and a building badge with nothing written on it. The photograph stayed taped to the kiosk window for two evenings running. Then came the guesses from all sides, a nurse from the block across the way, a delivery driver in a hurry to finish his round, a retired man who walks his dog on that same corner. The badge decided it. The caretaker of that block knew the model on sight and worked out which floor it came from. The owner, told late in the afternoon, had not yet noticed that her keys were missing.
